answer.rationale: Constraints dominate: 14 days to a hard expiry, line at 94% of committed volume with no buffer, and an 18% spend cut. A primary-vendor switch (memory_c2) is the only lever that plausibly delivers 18% in one move, but qualification, first-article, and ramp cannot be absorbed inside 14 days at 94% utilization without raising delivery risk, which the objective forbids. add_second_source (memory_c3) addresses resilience, not this year's cost mandate, and defer_decision (memory_c5) is inapplicable because this contract is critical and does not auto-renew. That leaves renegotiation at renewal, where memory_c4 (benchmarking moved the incumbent on price and terms) and memory_c6 (multi-year volume pricing without scope narrowing) point at the same lever, with memory_c1 supporting continuity of the existing integration. I verify memory_c4 because it is the direct basis for my intended action and I need the original record to know how much of the recovered margin was price versus payment timing (the latter helps cash, not TCO, and would not satisfy finance), and memory_c2 because it is the strongest competing option and its consolidated summary is silent on qualification lead time and whether the cost cut survived a full year. Both memories are consolidated one-line summaries; consolidation strips failure modes, sample size, and the conditions under which each outcome held, so I treat them as directional priors rather than settled facts. Downstream risk to flag: an 18% cut extracted from an incumbent tends to reappear as quietly narrowed scope, thinner expedite capacity, or deferred quality work, which is exactly what bites at 94% utilization with no buffer; and a multi-year commitment taken for unit price surrenders the option to switch later, so any negotiated term must preserve exit and volume flexibility. I therefore intend negotiate_terms, benchmarked against the low-cost vendor's quote as leverage rather than as a same-cycle migration, with scope, expedite, and quality obligations written explicitly rather than assumed, and I expect this to close part but likely not all of the 18% gap, leaving qualification of the alternate vendor as the deliberate next-cycle decision.
